body: Austria has long, white licence plates with the standard blue EU strip on the left.

Austria uses white bollards with a black top and a dark red or grey reflector, sometimes with a small black cap. These can be confused with Slovenian, Montenegrin, or German bollards, which have different reflector colors.
Austria uses two colour schemes for chevrons: white on red, and red on yellow.
Round wooden poles are the most common type of pole found in Austria.
Most of Austria is mountainous and covered in forests, while some areas in the east and northeast are much more flat and agricultural.
Alpine architecture is common in Austria, featuring houses with light-coloured walls, wooden elements like balconies, and dark, extended wooden roofs.
The official language of Austria is German, which uses special letters like Ä, Ö, Ü, and ß.
Austria primarily has Generation 3 and 4 coverage, distinguishing it from Germany (mostly Gen 4) and Switzerland (low-cam).
Austria has some Generation 4 'smallcam' coverage, which is mounted lower and has a large, sometimes transparent, circular blur.
Direction signs have a white background, a blue outline, and a unique font.
Town entrance signs are white with a blue outline and a unique font.
Green signs are common for directions to local facilities.
Pedestrian signs are unique for having two horizontal dashed lines instead of zebra stripes.
Road signs are sometimes mounted by four metal clips, a unique feature in central Europe.
Road markers are blue with white numbers and a recognizable decimal comma.
Austrian bus stop signs contain a yellow and green circle with the letter H.
One-way traffic signs with the word 'EINBAHN' are unique to Austria.
"No Stopping" and "No Waiting" signs often have the words "Anfang" or "Ende" written on them.
Simple dead-end signs with a white upside-down T are unique to Austria.
Yellow natural gas poles, resembling snow poles, are unique to Austria.
The central and western parts of Austria are the most mountainous, while flatter areas with rolling hills are found in the east.
Austrian A-roads generally increase in number from east to west.
Austrian B-roads also generally increase in number from east to west, with some exceptions in Vienna.
Each Austrian state has its own unique flag.
Each Austrian state has its own unique bus company with a distinct logo.
Bus stops with neon-yellow poles are found in Vorarlberg.
Yellow and white stripes around poles and signposts are found in Vorarlberg.
White kilometre markers can be found in Vorarlberg and western Salzburg.
A large white painted square can be found next to kilometre markers in Salzburg.
Green "Güterweg" signs are found in Burgenland.
White "Güterweg" signs with a black outline are mainly found in Upper Austria.
In Lower Austria, signs may have yellow and blue borders, matching the regional flag.
Vineyards are limited to the far eastern part of the country, especially near Vienna and Lake Neusiedl.
The highest parts of the Alps, with sharper peaks, are in the west and central parts of the country, particularly on the Italian border.
A unique tin foil antenna can be found in western Austria, mostly near the Swiss border.
Vienna street signs are recognizable dark blue plaques with a white serif font, and the number at the start indicates the district.
Many major cities have unique street signs, such as Salzburg's unique font or Klagenfurt's irregular white border.
Poles in Vienna and Innsbruck feature red-and-white tape. The tapes in Vienna are thinner and usually come in pairs.
Lake Constance (Bodensee), on the western border, is recognizable by its vastness compared to other Austrian lakes.
